cluster_genes.affinage_functional_annotation: ACTR5 is a conserved actin-related protein that functions as an essential subunit of the INO80 ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling complex, where it partners with IES6 to form a module that couples ATP hydrolysis to nucleosome sliding and histone H2A-H2B dimer exchange. The ACTR5-IES6 module engages nucleosomes through a grappler domain containing an arginine anchor required for nucleosome mobilization and a hydrophobic/acidic patch required for dimer displacement, and its unique insertion domains are necessary to convert ATPase activity into productive nucleosome movement [PMID:26306040, PMID:39676660]. Within the INO80 complex, ACTR5 contributes to homologous recombination-based DNA repair, YY1-dependent transcriptional activation, genome-wide nucleosome positioning at promoters, and regulation of cell cycle gene expression including CDKN2A [PMID:18026119, PMID:17721549, PMID:26755556, PMID:36563143]. Independent of INO80, ACTR5 suppresses myocardin-SRF-driven smooth muscle gene transcription by binding the RPEL motif of myocardin and the DNA-binding domain of SRF, and its expression is downregulated during muscle differentiation through alternative splicing coupled to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay [PMID:24567363, PMID:36977368].

BECN1 (Beclin 1) is a central scaffold protein of the class III PI3-kinase (PI3KC3/VPS34) complex that orchestrates autophagosome formation, endosomal trafficking, and regulated cell death. Its coiled-coil domain mediates homodimerization and heterodimerization with ATG14 or UVRAG to assemble distinct PI3KC3 subcomplexes, while its BARA domain undergoes partial β-sheet unfolding to anchor the complex on membranes; these activities are positively regulated by ULK1 phosphorylation at Ser30, AMPK phosphorylation at Thr388, JAK2 phosphorylation at Y333, SUMO3 conjugation at K380, and TRAF6-mediated K63-linked ubiquitination, and negatively regulated by BCL2/BCL2L1 binding to its BH3 domain, Rubicon/GLIPR2 binding to the BARA domain, CAMK2 phosphorylation at Ser295, CUL3–KLHL38- and RNF216-mediated K48-linked ubiquitination and degradation, and ISGylation at multiple lysines [PMID:17893711, PMID:27304906, PMID:29313410, PMID:34131122, PMID:30581147, PMID:31373534, PMID:33977871, PMID:27245989, PMID:33222586, PMID:25906440]. Beyond autophagy, AMPK-phosphorylated BECN1 directly binds SLC7A11 to block system Xc⁻ cystine transport and promote ferroptosis, and BECN1 facilitates adiponectin secretion through interaction with the exocyst complex and participates in retrograde endosome-to-Golgi trafficking [PMID:30057310, PMID:34038729, PMID:9105038, PMID:21183797]. Disruption of the BECN1–BCL2 interaction by the F121A knock-in mutation constitutively activates autophagy in vivo, sequestering amyloid-β oligomers and preventing Alzheimer's disease-like pathology in mice [PMID:28806762].

Cyclin D1 is the regulatory subunit of the CDK4/CDK6 holoenzyme that drives G1-to-S phase cell-cycle progression by phosphorylating pRb at specific residues (notably Ser780 and Thr826), thereby releasing E2F transcription factors to activate S-phase gene expression [PMID:8449399, PMID:9003781, PMID:9139732]. Assembly and nuclear import of cyclin D1–CDK4/6 complexes are promoted at substoichiometric concentrations by CIP/KIP family members (p21, p27, p57), whereas INK4 proteins (p16, p18, p19) competitively displace D-type cyclins from CDK4/6 to enforce G1 arrest [PMID:9106657, PMID:8259215, PMID:7739547]. Cyclin D1 protein turnover is controlled by GSK-3β-mediated Thr286 phosphorylation triggering nuclear export and proteasomal degradation, a pathway tonically suppressed by Ras/PI3K/Akt signaling, while K48-linked polyubiquitination is counteracted by the deubiquitinase USP10 [PMID:9832503, PMID:33184448]. Beyond its kinase-dependent roles, cyclin D1 functions as a CDK-independent transcriptional coactivator of the estrogen receptor, and CCND1 expression is itself regulated at the transcriptional level by diverse inputs including Wnt/β-catenin, NF-κB, CREB/VRK1, MAZ phase-separated condensates at promoter G-quadruplexes, and epigenetic marks (H3K27me3, H3S10ph), as well as post-transcriptionally by m6A modifications read by YTHDF3 and erased by FTO, and by miR-34a targeting of its 3′-UTR [PMID:9039267, PMID:38316778, PMID:35112553, PMID:18406353].

CDK10 is a cyclin-dependent serine/threonine kinase that suppresses oncogenic signaling, regulates ciliogenesis, and restrains innate immune activation through phosphorylation of diverse substrates. Activated by Cyclin M (FAM58A/CCNQ), CDK10 phosphorylates ETS2 to promote its proteasomal degradation, thereby repressing ETS2-driven c-RAF/MAPK signaling; loss of CDK10 de-represses this axis, conferring tamoxifen resistance in breast cancer and promoting metastasis in lung adenocarcinoma [PMID:18242510, PMID:24218572, PMID:37737453]. CDK10/Cyclin M also phosphorylates PKN2 at T121/T124 to stabilize RhoA and maintain actin architecture, suppressing primary cilia assembly [PMID:27104747], and phosphorylates DNMT1 and RAP80 to prevent accumulation of double-stranded RNA and R-loops that would otherwise trigger MDA5- and cGAS-dependent innate immune responses [PMID:41507536]. Bi-allelic loss-of-function mutations in CDK10 cause Al Kaissi syndrome characterized by growth retardation and skeletal defects, while mutations in its activating cyclin cause STAR syndrome [PMID:28886341, PMID:24218572].

CDK4 is a D-type cyclin-dependent serine/threonine kinase that functions as a master regulator of the G1-to-S phase cell cycle transition and integrates mitogenic, metabolic, and immune-regulatory signals. Upon binding D-type cyclins (assembled with the aid of CIP/KIP scaffold proteins p21/p27), CDK4 is activated by CAK/Cdk7-mediated phosphorylation of Thr172 and sequentially phosphorylates Rb to displace HDAC, relieve E2F-mediated transcriptional repression, and commit cells to S-phase entry; this activation is negatively regulated by INK4 family inhibitors (p16, p15, p18, p19) that compete with D-cyclins for CDK4 binding, modulated by Hsp90/Cdc37 chaperoning and Fkbp5-mediated prolyl isomerization of the T-loop [PMID:8449399, PMID:7935441, PMID:10499802, PMID:23622515, PMID:30485818]. Beyond Rb, CDK4 directly phosphorylates GCN5 to suppress hepatic gluconeogenesis, AMPKα2 to inhibit fatty acid oxidation, FLCN to regulate lysosomal mTORC1 recruitment, SPOP to stabilize PD-L1, EZH2 to activate STAT3-driven inflammatory gene expression, and CDC25A to generate a G1/S negative-feedback loop [PMID:24870244, PMID:29053957, PMID:31395606, PMID:29160310, PMID:32701505, PMID:28192398]. Germline CDK4 R24C mutations that abolish p16 binding cause familial melanoma susceptibility [PMID:8528263, PMID:7652577].

CWF19L1 is a nuclear splicing-associated protein that participates in both alternative splicing regulation and post-splicing intron lariat processing. It physically interacts with components of the U5 snRNP and the PRPF19 spliceosomal complex to control alternative splicing of immune-related and cell cycle genes, and CWF19L1 deficiency disrupts splicing patterns that impair T cell cytotoxic function [PMID:39542248]. CWF19L1 also directly binds the lariat RNA debranching enzyme DBR1 and localizes to nuclear domains adjacent to intron lariat spliceosome components, implicating it in intron turnover after splicing [PMID:25671812, PMID:41422678]. Loss-of-function mutations in CWF19L1 cause autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxia, with patient-derived cells showing loss of protein and zebrafish knockdown recapitulating cerebellar malformation and motor deficits [PMID:25361784].

Cytochrome c (CYCS) is a dual-function mitochondrial protein that serves as an essential electron carrier in the respiratory chain and as the obligate cytosolic trigger of the intrinsic apoptosis pathway. Upon apoptotic stimulation, cytochrome c is released from the mitochondrial intermembrane space into the cytosol — a process blocked by Bcl-2 and Bcl-xL — where it binds Apaf-1 and, together with dATP hydrolysis, drives Apaf-1 oligomerization into the apoptosome, recruiting and activating procaspase-9 at ~1:1 stoichiometry to initiate a hierarchical caspase cascade (caspases-3, -2, -6, -7, -8, -10) [PMID:8689682, PMID:9267021, PMID:10206961, PMID:9922454]. The pro-apoptotic activity of cytosolic cytochrome c is governed by its redox state — reduced cytochrome c is inactive and oxidation is required for apoptosome activation — and is negatively modulated by Hsp27, which sequesters released cytochrome c to block Apaf-1/procaspase-9 assembly [PMID:19029908, PMID:10980706]. Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in CYCS cause autosomal dominant thrombocytopenia through impaired mitochondrial respiratory chain function and aberrant megakaryocyte platelet release [PMID:30051457, PMID:27861742].

DDX52 is a nucleolar DEAD-box RNA helicase that drives ribosome biogenesis by coupling ATP hydrolysis to the remodeling of pre-ribosomal ribonucleoprotein complexes. In yeast, the ortholog Rok1 uses its ATPase activity to regulate release of the cofactor Rrp5 from pre-40S particles, thereby coordinating both 40S and 60S subunit assembly; snR30 snoRNA accumulation upon Rok1 loss is a secondary consequence of blocked Rrp5 displacement rather than direct snoRNA unwinding [PMID:27280440, PMID:18833290]. Rok1/DDX52 directly contacts pre-rRNA at expansion segment ES6 and multiple snoRNAs (snR30, snR10, U3, U14), and loss of DDX52 function reduces 47S precursor rRNA levels and arrests organismal growth in zebrafish, linking its molecular activity to whole-organism growth control [PMID:24947498, PMID:34323273]. Biochemically, human DDX52 is a 3′-to-5′ ATP-dependent translocase that unwinds DNA duplexes and DNA/RNA hybrids and possesses an IDR-dependent nucleic acid annealing activity; heterozygous loss in human cells impairs proliferation and migration, and DDX52 physically associates with c-Myc mRNA to sustain c-Myc signaling in cancer cells [PMID:41510705, PMID:34233596].

DUX4 is a double-homeodomain transcription factor that functions as a master activator of cleavage-stage embryonic gene programs and endogenous retroelements, with misexpression in skeletal muscle causing facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD) [PMID:28459457, PMID:22209328, PMID:18833193]. Its tandem homeodomains bind a bipartite TAAT-C-TAAT motif in a head-to-head orientation—with a primate-specific substitution conferring asymmetric sequence recognition—while its C-terminal domain recruits p300/CBP to acetylate H3K27 and pioneer inaccessible chromatin at MaLR/HERVL retrotransposons and HSATII pericentromeric repeats [PMID:30540931, PMID:26951377, PMID:24278031]. DUX4 suppresses interferon-γ-stimulated gene expression by physically engaging STAT1 through C-terminal (L)LxxL(L) motifs, reducing STAT1 and Pol II recruitment to ISG promoters, and blocks MHC class I induction [PMID:37092726, PMID:31727741]. In muscle, DUX4 represses MyoD and glutathione redox genes, triggers UPF1 degradation to inhibit nonsense-mediated mRNA decay, induces nuclear dsRNA foci from HSATII transcripts, and activates p53-independent but p38-dependent apoptotic pathways [PMID:18833193, PMID:25564732, PMID:31630170, PMID:31189728].

GGN (Gametogenetin) is a testis-enriched protein expressed in late pachytene spermatocytes and round spermatids that exists as multiple splice isoforms (GGN1, GGN2, GGN3) with distinct subcellular localizations: GGN1 at the nuclear membrane, GGN2 in the cytoplasm, and GGN3 in the nucleus/nucleoli [PMID:12574169]. GGN1 interacts with the germ cell protein POG and redirects its subcellular localization, and also physically associates with the Fanconi anemia/BRCA DNA repair components FANCL, FANCD2, and BRCC36 in mouse testis [PMID:12574169, PMID:23451117]. Complete Ggn knockout causes pre-implantation embryonic lethality, while heterozygous knockout pachytene spermatocytes accumulate unrepaired DNA double-strand breaks, establishing GGN as essential for male meiotic DSB repair and early embryonic development [PMID:23451117].

GTF2H1 encodes the p62 subunit of the ten-subunit general transcription factor IIH (TFIIH), a complex that couples RNA polymerase II transcription initiation with nucleotide excision repair (NER). Within the ring-like TFIIH core architecture, p62 serves as a structural scaffold that contacts and regulates the XPD helicase, and its pleckstrin homology (PH) domain provides a common recruitment interface through which both XPC (global genome repair) and UVSSA (transcription-coupled repair) deliver TFIIH to DNA lesions [PMID:29069470, PMID:30860024]. p62 also directly binds acidic transcriptional activation domains—including those of VP16, p53, and estrogen receptor α—thereby mediating activator-dependent stimulation of TFIIH-associated CDK7 kinase activity toward the RNA Pol II CTD [PMID:7935417, PMID:10949034]. GTF2H1 expression is positively regulated by SWI/SNF ATPases BRG1 and BRM, and its downregulation destabilizes the entire TFIIH complex, impairing both transcription and NER and sensitizing cells to platinum-based chemotherapy [PMID:30287812].

LRRC37A2 encodes a transmembrane leucine-rich repeat protein that undergoes cleavage and secretion, and whose overexpression induces filopodia formation in cultured cells [PMID:23064749]. In human substantia nigra, LRRC37A2 is expressed predominantly in astrocytes, where it promotes cellular migration and chemotaxis, modulates inflammatory responses, directly interacts with soluble α-synuclein, and co-localizes with Lewy bodies in Parkinson's disease brain tissue [PMID:35841044]. The gene arose through primate-lineage segmental duplications on chromosome 17q21.31, acquiring novel promoters that broadened its expression from an ancestrally testis-restricted pattern to include brain and other tissues [PMID:16625196, PMID:22419166]. LRRC37A2 expression is epigenetically regulated by DNA methylation at an exonic CpG site, with hypermethylation associated with transcriptional silencing in gastric cancer [PMID:33491552].

LRRC37B is a hominid-specific gene encoding a leucine-rich repeat receptor that localizes to the axon initial segment of human cortical pyramidal neurons, where it binds the secreted ligand FGF13A and the voltage-gated sodium channel β-subunit SCN1B to inhibit Nav channel function and reduce neuronal excitability [PMID:38134874]. The LRRC37B-containing low-copy repeats at 17q11.2 serve as substrates for nonallelic homologous recombination (NAHR), mediating recurrent ~1.0-Mb type-3 NF1 microdeletions associated with neurofibromatosis type 1 [PMID:20506354].

LYPD2 is a Ly6/PLAUR domain-containing protein whose direct molecular function and receptor targets remain uncharacterized. Co-expression and functional interaction assays in mouse hippocampus ruled out interaction with GluR2Q and GluR2R isoforms of the AMPA receptor, leaving its ionotropic receptor partners unidentified [PMID:36441793]. LYPD2 transcription is modulated by the HPV31 E8^E2 viral repressor in a phosphorylation-dependent manner, identifying it as a host gene target of viral transcription factor activity [PMID:29167339].

MAP4K2 (GCK) is a STE20-family serine/threonine kinase that functions as a critical upstream activator of the SAPK/JNK and p38 MAPK cascades, linking extracellular stimuli—TNF receptor engagement, bacterial PAMPs, and energy stress—to inflammatory gene expression, apoptotic regulation, and autophagy. In innate immunity, MAP4K2 couples TRAF2 and TLR signals to the MAP3Ks MEKK1 and MLK2/3 by promoting their oligomerization and autophosphorylation, and genetic ablation in mice renders macrophages defective in PAMP-driven cytokine release and confers resistance to endotoxin lethality [PMID:9712898, PMID:11784851, PMID:19246396]. Under energy stress, release from STRIPAK/STRN4-mediated inhibition enables MAP4K2 to phosphorylate LC3A at Ser87, driving autophagosome–lysosome fusion through the RAB3GAP–RAB18 axis in a YAP1-independent manner [PMID:37937799]. MAP4K2 kinase activity is required for the survival of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and RAS-mutant multiple myeloma cells, where it sustains JNK-dependent degradation of IKZF1/3, BCL-6, and c-MYC [PMID:27151888, PMID:33036022].

MED17 is an essential head-module subunit of the Mediator complex that bridges gene-specific transcription factors to the basal RNA Pol II machinery and integrates post-translational signals to control selective gene expression programs. Within the head module, MED17 functionally cooperates with Med6 and directly contacts RNA Pol II, TBP, TFIIB, TFIIE, and TFIIH subunits (XPB, XPG), and its integrity is required for Mediator association with active promoters and global transcription [PMID:9710620, PMID:16962561, PMID:25482373]. Signal-dependent phosphorylation tunes MED17's co-activator specificity: CK2-mediated phosphorylation at Ser53 drives insulin-stimulated lipogenic gene activation via USF1 recruitment, while MARK2-mediated phosphorylation at Ser152 selectively enhances NF-κB-dependent inflammatory transcription [PMID:28223413, PMID:33596087]. MED17 also contacts histone H4 tails, co-localizes with nucleotide excision repair factors after UV damage, and harbors pathogenic mutations (e.g., L371P) that cause Mendelian neurodevelopmental disease [PMID:22693636, PMID:25482373, PMID:20950787].

MED28 is a dual-compartment scaffolding protein that functions both as a subunit of the Mediator transcriptional co-activator complex and as a cytoplasmic signaling adaptor linking receptor-proximal kinases to downstream proliferative and migratory pathways. Within the nucleus, MED28 operates in the Mediator head module together with Med6, Med8, and Med18 to repress smooth muscle cell differentiation, maintain pluripotency through Oct4/Nanog expression, and regulate cell cycle progression at the G1–S transition and mitosis [PMID:17848560, PMID:26445504, PMID:30970566]. In the cytoplasm, MED28 associates with the actin cytoskeleton and the tumor suppressor merlin (NF2), is phosphorylated at Y64 by Src-family kinases (principally Lck) to create an SH2-binding motif for Grb2, and promotes cell migration and invasion through a MEK1–MMP2 axis and NF-κB–dependent EMT [PMID:15467741, PMID:16899217, PMID:22495818, PMID:27662245]. MED28 also activates Wnt/β-catenin signaling by suppressing the negative regulator HBP1 and promotes AKT/mTOR-dependent proliferation and lipogenesis in cancer cells [PMID:26660958, PMID:38619972].

MED4 is a core subunit of the mammalian Mediator complex (DRIP/ARC), a multisubunit transcriptional coactivator that bridges gene-specific activators—including nuclear receptors, SREBP-1a, VP16, and NF-κB—with the RNA polymerase II machinery to potentiate transcription on chromatin templates [PMID:10235266, PMID:10235267, PMID:15175163]. MED4 is essential for the viability of RB1-null retinoblastoma cells both in vitro and in orthotopic xenografts, establishing a synthetic lethal relationship between RB1 loss and MED4 loss that explains the reduced retinoblastoma penetrance in patients carrying large germline RB1 deletions encompassing the MED4 locus [PMID:24858910]. Beyond transcription, MED4 localizes to the centrosome as shown by BioID proximity labeling and immunofluorescence [PMID:25281560].

NAGK (N-acetyl-D-glucosamine kinase) is a sugar kinase that phosphorylates GlcNAc to GlcNAc-6-phosphate, feeding the hexosamine salvage pathway to maintain UDP-GlcNAc pools essential for glycosylation; under glutamine limitation, pancreatic cancer cells depend on this NAGK-driven salvage route for tumor growth [PMID:34844667]. Beyond its canonical sugar kinase activity, NAGK directly phosphorylates the N-acetylmuramic acid moiety of muramyl dipeptide (MDP) at C6, generating 6-O-phospho-MDP as the obligate NOD2 agonist required for innate immune sensing of bacterial peptidoglycan [PMID:36002575]. The UDP-GlcNAc salvage pathway including NAGK selectively promotes Wnt signaling during embryonic anteroposterior patterning, a role conserved across vertebrates and Drosophila [PMID:30904594].

NDUFA9 is an accessory subunit of mitochondrial respiratory chain Complex I that occupies the Q-module at the junction between the peripheral matrix arm and the membrane arm, where it is indispensable for late-stage Complex I assembly and activity. TALEN- and CRISPR-mediated knockout studies show that loss of NDUFA9 causes accumulation of incomplete membrane-arm subcomplexes while preventing incorporation of matrix-arm subunits, and re-expression rescues full Complex I assembly and oxidative phosphorylation [PMID:23223238, PMID:27626371]. NDUFA9 is a direct substrate of the mitochondrial deacetylase SIRT3, and its activity is further modulated by competing crotonylation (activating) and acetylation (inhibitory) post-translational modifications that tune Complex I function in contexts such as adipocyte thermogenesis [PMID:18794531, PMID:38657899]. Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in NDUFA9 cause Leigh syndrome with isolated Complex I deficiency [PMID:22114105, PMID:28671271].

NKTR encodes a 150 kDa surface protein on natural killer cells that contains an N-terminal hydrophobic region, a cyclophilin/peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase homology domain, and a hydrophilic C-terminus with arginine/serine-rich repeats, and functions as a component of a putative tumor-recognition complex required for NK-like cytotoxic activity [PMID:8421688, PMID:8144875]. Production of the full-length functional isoform is post-transcriptionally regulated by IL-2-controlled alternative pre-mRNA splicing that suppresses frameshifting splice variants in activated NK cells [PMID:8413330, PMID:9070924]. NKTR also acts as an upstream inhibitor of AKT phosphorylation, restraining G1/S cell cycle progression in non-small cell lung cancer cells [PMID:35537816].

NUBP2 is a cytosolic P-loop NTPase that functions as an essential scaffold for the assembly and transfer of iron-sulfur ([Fe-S]) clusters to cytosolic and nuclear Fe-S proteins, and additionally serves as a negative regulator of centriole duplication and ciliogenesis. NUBP2 forms a heterotetrameric complex with NUBP1 (NBP35) in which the conserved C-terminal CPXC motifs of both subunits coordinate a bridging [4Fe-4S] cluster; NUBP2 controls nucleotide binding order within the heterodimer, lacks intrinsic ATPase activity as a homodimer but becomes hydrolysis-competent when partnered with NUBP1, and increases the kinetic lability of assembled clusters on NUBP1 to facilitate transfer to target apoproteins via downstream CIA factors [PMID:17401378, PMID:22362766, PMID:30201724, PMID:30785732]. Independent of its Fe-S assembly role, NUBP2 localizes to centrioles and basal bodies and, together with NUBP1 and KIFC5A, restrains ciliogenesis and centriole reduplication; loss of NUBP2 causes supernumerary centrosomes, aberrant cilia formation, cranial neural crest apoptosis leading to craniofacial clefting, and primary microcephaly in mouse models and human patients [PMID:23807208, PMID:16638812, PMID:31733190].

PBXIP1 (HPIP) is a nucleo-cytoplasmic scaffolding protein that orchestrates multiple signaling cascades—including PI3K/AKT, MAPK/ERK, mTOR, and Wnt/LEF1—to drive cell proliferation, migration, epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), and lineage-specific differentiation. It localizes to microtubule-associated cytoskeletal fibers via an N-terminal leucine-rich region and undergoes CRM1-dependent nuclear export, enabling it to assemble cytoplasmic signaling complexes such as the full EGFR-RAS-ERK cascade and a FAK–calpain2 axis that controls focal adhesion turnover [PMID:12360403, PMID:37294756, PMID:25486428]. PBXIP1 also functions as a noncanonical guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) for Rab5 through two coiled-coil domains, cooperating with RUFY3 to promote β1-integrin endosomal trafficking and focal adhesion disassembly [PMID:37797694]. Its protein stability is regulated by MDM2/TBK1-dependent and RNF2-dependent ubiquitin–proteasome degradation, and it acts as a MYC transcriptional coactivator to rewire glutamine metabolism under glucose stress, while upstream its expression is controlled by a GATA1/CTCF complex and post-transcriptionally by miR-152 [PMID:24488098, PMID:34302919, PMID:22187427, PMID:29620271].

TARBP2 (TRBP) is a double-stranded RNA-binding protein that serves as a central cofactor in microRNA biogenesis, a direct inhibitor of PKR kinase signaling, and a post-transcriptional regulator of mRNA stability. Through its C-terminal Medipal domain, TRBP binds Dicer and recruits Ago2 to form the RISC-loading complex, enhancing pre-miRNA processing fidelity, modulating cleavage-site selection to produce isomiR variants, and acting as a gatekeeper that excludes non-substrate RNAs in crowded cellular environments [PMID:15973356, PMID:23006623, PMID:27934859, PMID:25557550]. TRBP inhibits PKR through direct dsRBD-mediated protein–protein interaction independently of RNA binding; under stress, phosphorylation-dependent dissociation of the TRBP–PACT heterodimer releases PACT to activate PKR, linking TRBP to innate immune and stress-response regulation [PMID:9034343, PMID:18936160, PMID:29348664]. Beyond the miRNA pathway, TRBP directly binds GC-rich structural elements in mRNAs to destabilize metastasis-suppressor and antiangiogenic transcripts in the cytoplasm, and in the nucleus recruits m6A methylation machinery and the nuclear exosome to degrade pre-mRNA targets [PMID:25043050, PMID:31300274, PMID:33484209].

TFDP1 encodes the transcription factor DP-1, an obligate heterodimerization partner of E2F-family proteins that together form the sequence-specific DNA-binding E2F/DP complex governing S-phase gene expression and cell cycle progression [PMID:8405995, PMID:8446173, PMID:8223441]. Heterodimerization occurs through the hydrophobic heptad repeat and marked box domains; the resulting complex activates transcription of cyclins A and E, CDK2, and DHFR, and is negatively regulated by pRb (which contacts both E2F1 and DP-1 marked box domains), cyclin A/CDK2-mediated phosphorylation that inhibits DNA binding, ARF (which directly binds free DP-1 to disrupt E2F1/DP-1 heterodimerization independently of p53), and Kbtbd5-mediated ubiquitination and degradation of DP-1 [PMID:16360038, PMID:7969176, PMID:16135794, PMID:25940086]. Nuclear import of the E2F1/TFDP1 complex requires KPNA2, and unpartnered DP-1 is retained in the cytoplasm and targeted for ubiquitin-dependent degradation [PMID:31783876, PMID:9989809]. Beyond canonical cell cycle gene regulation, TFDP1 modulates global chromatin accessibility through transcriptional control of canonical histones [PMID:38361031].

TRAPPC6A is a core subunit of the TRAPP I, II, and III vesicle-tethering complexes that facilitates ER-to-Golgi membrane trafficking and complex assembly by forming a heterodimer with BET3 (resolved at 2.2 Å), thereby promoting BET3's incorporation into TRAPP and its interaction with other subunits such as BET5 and TRAPPC2L [PMID:16262728, PMID:32843486]. Loss of TRAPPC6A function disrupts melanosome biogenesis, causing mosaic hypopigmentation and abnormal melanosomes in mice [PMID:16697553], and a missense mutation in TRAPPC6A causes intellectual disability and dysmorphic features in humans, linked to impaired proteasome-dependent turnover and aberrant protein stabilization [PMID:29391579]. An alternatively spliced isoform (TRAPPC6AΔ) undergoes Ser35 phosphorylation-dependent polymerization regulated by WWOX, induces caspase-3 activation and amyloid-β production, and modulates influenza A virus M2 protein trafficking to the plasma membrane [PMID:25650666, PMID:27795429].

USP6 (TRE17) is a hominoid-specific deubiquitinating enzyme that couples ubiquitin-specific protease activity with small GTPase signaling to regulate receptor surface abundance, transcriptional programs, and tumorigenesis. Its N-terminal TBC domain binds GDP-bound Arf6 and promotes Arf6 activation rather than acting as a canonical Rab GAP, while Ca²⁺/calmodulin binding to this domain regulates USP6 monoubiquitination [PMID:15509780, PMID:16127172]. The C-terminal USP domain deubiquitylates multiple substrates—Frizzled receptors to amplify Wnt signaling, Jak1 to activate STAT3, c-Jun to enhance AP-1-driven invasion, NMDA receptor subunits to promote synaptic plasticity, and clathrin-independent endocytosis cargo to counteract MARCH E3 ligase-mediated lysosomal targeting [PMID:27162353, PMID:27440725, PMID:29061731, PMID:31841517, PMID:25179595]. Transcriptional upregulation of USP6 through promoter-swapping chromosomal translocations drives bone and soft tissue tumors (including aneurysmal bone cysts) via USP-dependent NF-κB activation through an atypical IKKα/IKKβ-dependent but IκB-independent mechanism, MMP-9/10 induction through RhoA-ROCK signaling, and suppression of osteoblast maturation through BMP-4 downregulation and Gremlin-1 upregulation [PMID:22081069, PMID:20418905, PMID:20864534].

USP7 is a cysteine deubiquitinase that functions as a master regulator of protein stability across the p53-MDM2 axis, DNA damage response, chromatin regulation, and multiple developmental and oncogenic signaling pathways. Its catalytic domain is intrinsically autoinhibited and requires activation by its C-terminal ubiquitin-like domains (HUBL-45), with further allosteric hyperactivation by GMPS; substrates are recruited primarily through a P/A/ExxS motif that binds the N-terminal TRAF-like domain, which is also exploited by viral proteins such as EBNA1 and KSHV vIRF4 [PMID:16474402, PMID:21981925, PMID:22056774]. USP7 deubiquitinates and stabilizes p53 directly, yet preferentially stabilizes MDM2 and MDMX under basal conditions, establishing a dynamic feedback loop in which CK2 phosphorylation maintains USP7 stability and DNA damage triggers ATM/PPM1G-mediated dephosphorylation to shift the balance toward p53 activation [PMID:11923872, PMID:15053880, PMID:15916963, PMID:22361354]. Beyond p53 signaling, USP7 deubiquitinates substrates spanning chromatin regulation (EZH2, H2BK120ub1, RNF168, KDM5B), DNA repair and replication (Chk1, Rad18, MCM-BP, RRM2), and key signaling effectors (PTEN, FOXO4, HIF-1α, β-catenin, KRAS, YAP/TAZ, Gli, NOTCH1, Raf-1), thereby influencing cell cycle progression, the Hedgehog and Hippo pathways, Wnt signaling, and immune checkpoint regulation [PMID:18716620, PMID:25894431, PMID:25961918, PMID:33849069, PMID:30679505, PMID:39499616, PMID:26120032, PMID:27934968]. USP7 knockout is embryonic lethal in mice, partially rescued by p53 deletion, confirming both p53-dependent and p53-independent essential functions in vivo [PMID:19946331, PMID:21350561].

ZEB2 is a multi-zinc finger transcription factor that functions as a master regulator of cell identity transitions across epithelial, neural, hematopoietic, immune, and vascular lineages, primarily by repressing lineage-inappropriate gene programs. ZEB2 represses E-cadherin, cyclin D1, ephrinB2, and other target genes by binding E-box and related promoter elements, recruiting the NuRD/HDAC1 corepressor complex to mediate transcriptional silencing, while also acting as a transcriptional activator of select targets (e.g., cadherin-11, ACSL4, ETS1) through cooperation with Sp1 or direct E-box engagement [PMID:11430829, PMID:17855508, PMID:18182442, PMID:36951067, PMID:24130169]. ZEB2 operates within a double-negative feedback loop with the miR-200 family—each repressing the other's expression—and its protein levels are further controlled by the Zeb2-NAT antisense transcript that promotes its translation, by ubiquitin-proteasome-mediated degradation, and by upstream transcription factors including HIF-1α, NFIL3, C/EBPs, FoxQ1, and MEF2A [PMID:18829540, PMID:17585049, PMID:29311544, PMID:21727196, PMID:35732734]. In the immune system, ZEB2 drives age-associated B cell and terminal effector CD8+ T cell differentiation, specifies cDC2 fate through an Nfil3-Zeb2-Id2 circuit, programs tumor-associated macrophage identity, and is required broadly for hematopoietic lineage output; in the nervous system it controls cortical interneuron migration (via Unc5b repression), axonal growth (via ninein), Schwann cell myelination, Bergmann glia specification, and astrogliosis [PMID:38271512, PMID:29449309, PMID:31406377, PMID:40215981, PMID:23312517, PMID:25741725, PMID:27294512, PMID:32610135].

ZNF322 is a C2H2 Krüppel-like zinc-finger transcription factor that activates MAPK-responsive transcriptional elements (SRE and AP-1) and directly binds the Shh promoter to upregulate sonic hedgehog expression [PMID:15555580, PMID:32929330]. In the context of oncogenic Kras signaling, YY1 binds and activates the ZNF322 promoter, and the resulting ZNF322-driven Shh upregulation stimulates endothelial pro-angiogenic responses that promote lung cancer neo-angiogenesis [PMID:32929330]. ZNF322 expression is post-transcriptionally repressed by miR-4317 targeting its 3′UTR, and ZNF322 silencing suppresses gastric cancer cell proliferation and S-G2/M cell cycle progression [PMID:28880489].
